description:
Four sub-species have been recorded from Ireland.
In subsp. erectum and subsp. microcarpum the mature fruit is dark brown or black above (paler below) and distinctly shouldered. In the former the shoulder is flat-topped and 4–6 mm at its widest point; the shoulder of the latter is more rounded and narrower (2.5–4.5 mm).
The uniformly pale-brown fruits of subsp. neglectum (2–4.5 mm) taper to the beak. Many of the similar but longer (4–7 mm) pale-brown subglobose fruits of subsp. oocarpum fail to mature.

description: In addition to P. ×zizii, described below, two other hybrids of this species are known from Ireland. P. × salicifolius is the hybrid with P. perfoliatus; it differs from P. lucens chiefly in its stalkless leaves. P. × nerviger is the hybrid with P. alpinus; it is known only from the River Fergus in Co. Clare.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: The only fertile hybrid in the genus.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Hybrids with P. coloratus (P. × lanceolatus) and P. natans (P. × variifolius) are known. The former  is locally frequent in the Caher River, Co. Clare.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Hybrids with the next species (P. × suecicus) have recently been reported from four widely scattered sites in the west, three of which are lakes. The hybrid is similar to P. pectinatus, but some of the stipules form a tube, the pollen is sterile and no fruit is set. It is likely to be found elsewhere.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Most of the Irish plants have ‘double’ flowers, with some of the stamens replaced by extra petals
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Hybrids between the previous two species are occasionally found. They have flowers of various shades of pink.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Flowers of Irish plants require investigation to determine the frequency of dioecy.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: A variable plant, represented in Ireland by two fairly distinct sub-species, though intermediates can be found:
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Rare specimens, with the hairs confined to a single line on the flowering stems and only found on river margins and flood plains, have sometimes been distinguished as a separate sub-species – subsp. holosteoides. All other plants are assigned to subsp. vulgare.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: C. tomentosum, widely grown for ornament, and occasionally more or less naturalised near gardens, is generally similar, but the whole plant is white with densely matted, non-glandular hairs.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Similar to Stellaria neglecta or to luxuriant plants of Stellaria media in general appearance, but distinct in its unlobed, unnotched petals and leaves with 3 unbranched veins.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Typically plants have a flask-shaped capsule, with a broad base and a narrow neck. Plants with a conical capsule, not markedly narrowed at the neck, and often with a more delicate, less bushy habit, may be distinguished as subsp. leptoclados.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Not found in Britain, but very similar plants are known from the Arctic and the mountains of Central Europe.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Plants with a hairless ovary and upper leaves in 2 ranks from County Antrim may correspond to E. leptochila, confirmation is desirable. Plants differing from E. helleborine in their greyish-green, lilac-tinged leaves and flowers with a rather long, narrow labellum have also been found in that county: some have the upper leaves in 2 ranks and a hairy ovary, others have spirally arranged upper leaves and a hairless ovary. In Ireland the group would benefit from further investigation.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Three sub-species are recognised in Britain, but further work is needed to confirm their occurrence in Ireland. In subsp. conopsea the spur is 12–14 mm long with a deeply lobed labellum up to 6.5 mm long and wide and the lobes equal in length; the flowers of subsp. borealis have a labellum which is narrow (4 mm wide) and scarcely lobed with the mid-lobe longer than the laterals; whereas subsp. densiflora has a dense spike of flowers, a spur 10–16 mm long and a deeply lobed labellum 6.5–8 mm wide, wider than long and which has the mid-lobe shorter than the laterals.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: D. maculata is directly derived from D. fuchsii by chromosome doubling. Naturally, these species look similar and some specimens of these species are almost indistinguishable. However, in Ireland D. maculata is represented only by the narrow-leaved form of the species, subsp. ericetorum described above, which makes for easy separation from the broader-leaved D. fuchsii and its sub-species. They are also separable on habitat features as D. maculata subsp. ericetorum is characteristic of heaths and bogs whilst D. fuchsii is found in drier, less acid situations.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: There are 2 distinct sub-species and two varieties.The above description applies to subsp. fuchsia. Plants lacking pigmentation, found on limestone grassland in the west with white flowers and unspotted leaves and sometimes with the central lobe of the labellum equalling in length the broader laterals are a distinct variety var. okellyi (Orchis okellyi, D. fuchsii subsp. okellyi).
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Plants found on machair and cliff-tops, differing from subsp. fuchsii in that they are shorter and have darker pink flowers with a rather wide labellum (up to 17 mm) with the lateral lobes themselves toothed and a stout spur constitute a second sub-species – subsp. hebridensis.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: subsp. traunsteinerioides (D. traunsteinerioides, D. traunsteineri) has usually no more than 4 leaves which are very narrow and usually 7–9 times as long as wide which, if spotted, have the markings as transverse bars. The flower spike is lax, containing no more than 15 flowers. The flowers are large with the labellum deltate in shape and deeply 3-lobed with mid-lobe greatly exceeding the laterals. The spur is stout and cylindrical up to 12 mm long. Fens, flushes and wet areas in machair; mostly in the centre and north-east and often overlooked.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Purple-flowered populations are attributable to subsp. incarnata var. pulchella; var. haematodes has rather narrower leaves spotted on one side only; it occurs sporadically throughout the range of the species  var. hyphaematodes (attributed in the past to D. incarnata subsp. cruenta) from fens in western Ireland also has narrower leaves though they are spotted on both sides.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: The above description applies to the widespread subsp. majalis var. majalis. Most populations of D. majalis have hybridized with D. maculata and are highly variable. Some populations have at times been regarded as distinct and are called D. kerryensis, which includes D. majalis subsp. occidentalis (D. occidentalis). These plants are shorter with darker flowers and have a labellum of equal lobes; var. brevifolia (D. purpurella) has simple spots on the leaves, sometimes confined to the tip, rich-purple flowers, a more or less unlobed labellum and a tapering spur.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Recently, sometimes treated, on the basis of molecular evidence, as a species of Anacamptis – Anacamptis morio.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Very variable, but no satisfactory classification of the variants has been devised.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Nearly all plants in Britain are female; rare hermaphrodite plants do occur, however. In Ireland further investigation is required; only female plants have so far been recorded.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: The hybrid between R. japonica and R. sachalinensis (R. × bohemica) is intermediate in leaf shape and leaf size, and is very likely under-recorded in Ireland, being known largely from the south. In Britain both functionally female and, somewhat less commonly, functionally male plants have been recorded. Irish plants require further investigation.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Variants found on sand-dunes by the west coast are sometimes distinguished as subsp. hibernicus. They have short stems and short, compact inflorescences; the leaves are rather fleshy and scabrid-puberulent with stiff, very short hairs especially on the petioles. All other material belongs to subsp. acetosa.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: The common sub-species is subsp. crispus. Very tall plants, usually found on estuarine mud, with a large fruit (at least 2.5 mm) and a panicle rather lax in fruit, are distinguished as subsp. uliginosus. Shorter plants with exceptionally dense fruiting heads found on shingle, salt-marshes and maritime dunes have been separated as subsp. littoreus.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Hybrids with R. crispus are fairly frequent. They are intermediate in characters of leaf and fruit, and are nearly, but not completely, sterile. Some other hybrids have been recorded in the genus, but are much rarer.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Erratic in appearance as dependent on low water levels for germination on exposed soil.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Armeria plants have either rough or smooth pollen and possess either a rough or smooth stigma. However, unlike Primula, these differences are less obvious and visible only with a good hand-lens or microscope.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: This is an apomictic species in which a number of segregate groups can be recognised. L. recurvum subsp. portlandicum has been recorded from North Kerry; L. recurvum subsp. pseudotranswallianum (previously recorded in error as L. transwallianum) from Clare and L. recurvum subsp. humile (previously recorded in error as L. paradoxum) from Donegal. Plants recorded as L. binervosum agg. in the past are probably L. recurvum. Recent evidence suggests, however, that the distinctions between these taxa and between them and L. procerum are small and grouping these taxa under the L. binervosum agg. may be the most appropriate treatment.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: R. × anceps, the hybrid between R. sylvestris and R. amphibia, is intermediate in most characters. It differs from R. sylvestris in its widely spreading fruiting pedicels, short flask-like fruits, stem-leaves which are more shallowly lobed at their apex than their base and from R. amphibia in its deeply divided stem-leaves [Fig. 82f]. Occasional; in similar habitats to its parents, though often in their absence; apparently absent from the north-east, centre-west and south-west, but probably overlooked.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: A taxonomically complex group which requires investigation in Ireland and comparison with British and Continental plants.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: A. brownii (A. ciliata) differs in being nearly hairless, except for a few stiff hairs on the leaf-margins; also the stem-leaves are often not clasping. It is probably best regarded as a variety of A. hirsuta. Sand-dunes on the west coast; rare.
creator: Parnell, John
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: differs in the basal leaves, which are not fleshy, and capsule which is usually narrowed at both ends and occurs on rocks and by streams in the higher mountains.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: with flowers 5–6 mm across; petals less than 4 mm long; upper leaves almost stalkless, not clasping the stem and with the fruit variable in shape, often ovoid, often narrowed at both ends, sometimes globose, occurs on rocks, cliffs, salt-marshes and occasionally sandy areas near the coast.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Hybrids with the previous species are intermediate in morphology and fairly frequently recorded. The frequency with which they really do occur is difficult to determine, however, because the parent species are themselves so variable. It appears essential, unfortunately, to count the chromosomes to be certain of hybridity.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: The cultivated turnip in Ireland is subsp. rapifera and the cultivated Rape is subsp. oleifera.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Brassica rapa subsp. rapa is known as White turnip in Ireland.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Often identified in error as Brassica nigra, and distinguishable from it only in fruit, when the seedless upper portion of the fruit of B. nigra is distinctive.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: subsp. raphanistrum is an occasional weed of sandy or peaty fields; it is annual, usually with whitish flowers and fruits no more than 5 mm wide.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: subsp. maritimus (R. maritimus) is frequent on sandy and shingle shores, and very abundant in places; it is biennial with yellow (sometimes white) flowers and fruits more than 5 mm wide
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: The cultivated Radish is R. sativus
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: All Irish material is thought to belong to subsp. piloselloides, a weakly defined sub-species with relatively large and sparsely hairy leaves. The distinctions between the sub-species are generally not clear, however, and the relationship of Irish plants to that of the same sub-species in the Pyrenees requires investigation.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Recent molecular evidence suggests that Lavatera may be better amalgamated with the genus Malva, with the above species thus becoming Malva arborea; however, we have decided to keep the genera separate for the time being.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: A. campestre, the Field maple, a fair-sized tree, but usually seen as a shrub; is occasionally planted in hedges and rarely naturalised. It has smaller leaves, with obtuse, entire lobes, the flowers are in erect panicles, and both wings of the fruit lie in the same straight line and the older twigs are ridged.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: A. platanoides, the Norway maple, is often planted and is naturalised in woods and hedges in a few places. It has leaves like those of A. pseudoplatanus, but with finely pointed lobes and milky sap in the leaf-stalk. The yellowish flowers in erect panicles appear before the leaves and the buds are reddish.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: The variety most commonly planted, with fat, nearly spherical buds (‘Riccartonii’), hardly ever sets fruit and is naturalised only occasionally. Other forms, with narrower buds, are planted in a few districts and are becoming naturalised.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: In some Irish plants the leaf-stalks appear almost equally pubescent all-round, but in many cases the leaf-stalks are more densely hairy on the upper surface. Further investigation of Irish plants is required.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: A hybrid between C. lutetiana and C. alpina; the latter does not now occur in Ireland, but probably did in the past.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Now commonly accepted as distinguished from Epilobium on the basis of molecular and morphological features, including its alternate leaves, slightly zygomorphic flowers, individual pollen grains and absence of an extension of the base of the flower (= hypanthium) above the base of the ovary.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Though currently rare, we have included this species as it is likely to spread.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Plants are heterostylous – different plants bear flowers of one of three forms which differ in the relative lengths of the style and stamens.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: (Cultivated flax) was formerly cultivated for linen, especially in the north-east, and occurs rarely as a casual. It is like L. bienne but has broader leaves and larger, bright blue flowers.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: Flowers which do not open (cleistogamous) are usually produced in spring to early summer.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.

description: O. debilis, similar to O. articulata but rather larger and less hairy in all its parts, with flowers 15–20 mm across, is an occasionally naturalised casual.
source: Parnell J., Curtis T. & Cullen E. 2012. Webb’s an Irish Flora. [8th ed.] Cork: Cork University Press.
